title: Faith Yields, Sight Chooses
summary: Returning to his altar, Abram ends a family quarrel by yielding first choice to Lot, who chooses Sodom’s plain, while God renews the promise of land and seed.
historicalContext: Abram comes back from Egypt richer than he went down, now a seminomadic chief whose flocks, herds, and servants need wide pasture and dependable water. The hill country of central Canaan was already held by Canaanite towns and by Perizzite villagers in the open country, so grazing and wells were limited and easily disputed. From the ridge near Bethel, nearly three thousand feet above sea level, a herdsman could look down toward the Jordan rift, a low, warm, spring-fed basin that appeared lush beside the rain-dependent highlands. The cities of that plain, Sodom and Gomorrah among them, lay near the southern end of what is now the Dead Sea and were later overthrown in judgment. Hebron, where Abram finally settles, stood on the high southern ridge route and became the family’s long-term home and burial place.
literaryContext: Chapter 13 answers the failure of 12:10–20. Abram, who fled to Egypt and endangered Sarai, retraces his steps to the altar at Bethel and calls again on the LORD; the chapter closes with another altar at Mamre, so worship frames the whole account. Between those altars stands a carefully balanced contrast. Lot “lifted up his eyes” and chose for himself; afterward the LORD tells Abram to lift up his eyes and receive what is given. Two narrator’s asides, the Canaanite presence in verse 7 and Sodom’s wickedness in verse 13, shade the decision. The key verbs “dwell,” “separate,” and “see” bind the story together, and the promise of land and offspring from 12:1–7 is widened. The episode prepares for Lot’s capture in chapter 14 and the destruction of Sodom in chapters 18–19.
themes: Returning to the place of worship after failure
Prosperity as a test of character
Choosing by sight versus living by promise
God’s renewed gift of land and offspring
Pilgrim life anchored at the altar

outline.title: Back to the Altar at Bethel
outline.summary: Abram leaves Egypt with his household and wealth and returns by stages to the first altar, where he calls on the LORD again.

outline.title: Strife and a Generous Offer
outline.summary: Abundant flocks crowd the land, the herdsmen quarrel, and Abram refuses strife between kinsmen by giving Lot first choice.

outline.title: Lot Chooses the Plain
outline.summary: Lot sees the well-watered Jordan plain, chooses it for himself, and moves toward Sodom, whose men were exceedingly wicked.

outline.title: The Promise Enlarged
outline.summary: After the separation the LORD shows Abram the whole land, promises it to him and his seed for ever, and bids him walk through it.

outline.title: A New Altar at Mamre
outline.summary: Abram moves his tent to the oaks of Mamre at Hebron and builds an altar to the LORD.

verses.bibleText: And Abram went up out of Egypt, he, and his wife, and all that he had, and Lot with him, into the south.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The scene in Egypt closes with Pharaoh’s men escorting Abram to the border, and this verse records the return without a word of explanation or conversation. “Went up” fits the terrain, for the road climbs from the Nile delta through the wilderness to the higher ground of southern Canaan, but the phrase also marks a reversal. Abram had gone “down into Egypt” in fear (12:10); now he goes up toward the land God had promised. The destination is “the south,” the Negeb, the dry region where he had been travelling before the famine drove him away (12:9). He resumes the journey at the point where he left it.

The inventory is complete: “he, and his wife, and all that he had.” Sarai is restored to him, and nothing has been lost, although Abram’s scheme had placed both his marriage and the promise in danger. That outcome is the work of God, who struck Pharaoh’s house to protect her (12:17; Psalm 105:14–15). The patriarch leaves Egypt preserved by mercy, not by his own cleverness.

Lot is named last, almost as an afterthought, after the household and possessions. The placement prepares for what follows, since Lot and his property are about to become the subject of the story. The departure also anticipates a later exodus, when Abram’s descendants would go up out of Egypt carrying wealth, after plagues had fallen on the royal house (Exodus 12:35–38). The God who brought Abram out would bring Israel out, and in the fullness of time would call his own Son out of Egypt (Matthew 2:15).

wordNotes.explanation: The verb ʿalah describes ascent, and travel from Egypt to Canaan is regularly called going up because the land rises from the Nile valley to the hill country. It stands opposite the “went down” (yarad) of 12:10, framing the Egyptian episode. The same pairing returns when Jacob’s family goes down to Egypt and Israel later goes up out of it.

Negeb names the arid southern region of Canaan around and beyond Beersheba, a land of seasonal pasture rather than settled farming. Because Canaan lies north of Egypt, the term here designates a region, not merely a compass direction. Abram had been moving toward the Negeb when the famine struck.

verses.bibleText: And Abram was very rich in cattle, in silver, and in gold.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Abram was very rich in cattle, in silver, and in gold.” The order of the list matters. Livestock comes first because it was the measure of wealth for a man living in tents, and because the coming conflict will arise over pasture, not precious metal. This is also the first time Scripture mentions silver and gold together as marks of riches. Some of this wealth had come from Pharaoh, who “entreated Abram well” for Sarai’s sake (12:16), and Egypt was renowned in the ancient world for its gold.

The Hebrew word rendered “rich” literally means heavy, and the same word described the famine that was “grievous” in the land (12:10). The narrator may intend the echo. Abram had gone to Egypt to escape a heavy famine and came back weighed down with goods. The wealth was real blessing, part of God’s promise to make him great (12:2), yet it had been gained in circumstances that reflected little credit on Abram, and it will immediately bring a new trial. Abundance tests faith as surely as scarcity does.

Scripture does not condemn Abram for being rich, and later it credits God with the increase (24:35). What the narrative examines is how riches will affect his relationships and his choices. Jesus would later warn that possessions can choke the word and draw the heart away from God (Mark 4:19; Matthew 6:21). In Abram’s case the question of the chapter is whether wealth will divide the family of promise, and whether the man who failed under pressure in Egypt will now act from faith.

wordNotes.explanation: Kaved means heavy or weighty and, by extension, burdened with goods, hence rich. Context decides the sense: the same adjective describes the grievous famine in 12:10 and the heavy hands of Moses in Exodus 17:12. The related noun kavod can mean honour or glory, the weight of a person’s standing. Here the word stresses the sheer quantity of Abram’s possessions.

verses.bibleText: And he went on his journeys from the south even to Beth-el, unto the place where his tent had been at the beginning, between Beth-el and Hai;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abram does not rush north. “He went on his journeys from the south,” moving by stages, from one pasture and watering place to the next, as a herdsman with large flocks must. The goal of these stages is precise: Beth-el, “unto the place where his tent had been at the beginning, between Beth-el and Hai.” The wording deliberately recalls 12:8, where Abram first pitched his tent on the ridge east of Bethel and built an altar.

The repetition of “at the beginning” here and “at the first” in the next verse underlines a return to the starting point of his walk with God in the land. Abram retraces his route to the site where he had last known the LORD’s presence before he left for Egypt. Physical return accompanies spiritual return. The prophet would later urge Israel to ask for “the old paths” and walk in them (Jeremiah 6:16); Abram does exactly that.

The name Beth-el means “house of God,” though in Abram’s day the town was known as Luz and received the name Bethel from Jacob’s experience there (28:19). Moses uses the familiar later name so his readers can locate the place. Its association with God’s presence makes it a fitting destination for a man who needs to recover his bearings. A pilgrim who strays does well to go back to the place of his first commitment.

wordNotes.explanation: The noun massaʿ comes from the verb for pulling up tent pegs and setting out, and denotes a stage of travel. The plural pictures a journey made in successive camps rather than a single march. The same term describes Israel’s wilderness stages from one encampment to another, suggesting a pattern of pilgrim travel.

verses.bibleText: Unto the place of the altar, which he had made there at the first: and there Abram called on the name of the LORD.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Verse 4 completes the sentence: Abram comes “unto the place of the altar, which he had made there at the first: and there Abram called on the name of the LORD.” During the whole Egyptian episode there was no altar, no prayer, and no word from God recorded. Abram schemed, feared, and prospered, but he did not worship. Now the silence is broken at the very place where worship had last been offered. The altar is both a memorial of God’s earlier promise and a fresh beginning.

The text records no speech of repentance, yet the action speaks. To go back to the altar is to acknowledge that the right relationship with God had been interrupted and needed to be restored. Calling on the name of the LORD involved prayer and sacrifice, and it also had a public side. Since the days of Seth, those who called on the LORD’s name confessed him openly (4:26). In a land full of Canaanite shrines, Abram’s altar declared to his neighbours which God he served and gave them opportunity to learn of him.

This return explains the change in Abram that follows. The man who acted from fear in Egypt will act from generosity toward Lot. Worship restores perspective: it reminds the worshipper that his security rests in God’s promise, not in his own management of events. The chapter will end, as it begins, at an altar (13:18), and between those two altars Abram is able to yield, to wait, and to receive.

Grace stands behind the scene. God does not reject Abram for his failure or withdraw the promise; he receives the returning worshipper. The pattern anticipates the gospel invitation, “whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Romans 10:13), and the assurance that the Father welcomes those who come back (Luke 15:20). An important consideration for any home or journey is whether it keeps a person near the place of the altar.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּקְרָא … בְּשֵׁם יְהוָה (wayyiqraʾ … beshem YHWH) — called on the name of the LORD
wordNotes.explanation: This expression describes worship addressed to the LORD by his revealed name, including prayer and sacrifice, and in several passages it also carries the sense of proclaiming that name. It first appears in the days of Enosh and becomes characteristic of Abram’s altars. Joel and Paul apply it to the saving call of faith.

verses.bibleText: And Lot also, which went with Abram, had flocks, and herds, and tents.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Lot now moves to the centre of the story. He is described as the one “which went with Abram,” a reminder that he had shared the journey from Haran (12:4) and evidently the sojourn in Egypt as well. His wealth is listed as “flocks, and herds, and tents”: sheep and goats, cattle, and the many tents needed for servants and dependants. Abram is called “very rich”; Lot simply “also had.” The nephew’s prosperity is real but secondary.

That prosperity was in large part the overflow of God’s blessing on Abram. The promise that those who bless Abram would be blessed (12:3) was already at work in Lot’s life while he stayed in Abram’s company. Lot’s welfare was bound up with his nearness to the man God had chosen, a point that makes his coming decision more significant. Travelling with the people of promise brings benefit, yet a person may share the journey for years without making the promise his own.

wordNotes.term: צֹאן־וּבָקָר וְאֹהָלִים (tson-uvaqar weʾohalim) — flocks, and herds, and tents
wordNotes.explanation: Tson covers small livestock, sheep and goats together, while baqar means cattle. Adding “tents” (ʾohalim) indicates a sizeable household of herdsmen and servants, since each tent represented people as well as shelter. Wealth among pastoralists was counted in animals and the dependants who tended them.

verses.bibleText: And the land was not able to bear them, that they might dwell together: for their substance was great, so that they could not dwell together.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the land was not able to bear them, that they might dwell together.” The problem is stated twice in one verse, once in terms of the land and once in terms of the people: “their substance was great, so that they could not dwell together.” The repetition emphasises how serious the impasse had become. The verb “dwell” recurs through the chapter, and here it is twice negated. Two households that had travelled as one could no longer share the same hillsides.

The cause is surprising. A famine had driven Abram away from Canaan; now abundance creates the crisis. The hill country around Bethel was partly wooded and already occupied, so pasture and water for two great herds were limited. Blessing itself, multiplied beyond what the available ground could support, set the stage for strife. The same pressure would arise again between Jacob and Esau, whose possessions also became “more than that they might dwell together” (36:7).

There is a sober lesson here. Prosperity brings its own temptations, and families that hold together under hardship sometimes divide over property. Material increase calls for more grace, not less. Paul’s counsel that godliness with contentment is great gain (1 Timothy 6:6–10) applies directly. The narrative also raises a quiet question for Israel’s later readers: if this land could not hold two herdsmen together, how would it hold a nation? The answer lies in God’s promise, which the chapter will soon renew.

wordNotes.explanation: The common verb nasaʾ means to lift or carry; applied to land it describes the capacity to support people and herds. The ground is pictured as a bearer whose load had become too great. The identical expression recurs in the account of Jacob and Esau’s separation.

Rekhush denotes movable property, goods and livestock gathered over time, as distinct from land. It described what Abram brought from Haran in 12:5. God later promises that Abram’s descendants would come out of their affliction “with great substance,” using the same noun.

verses.bibleText: And there was a strife between the herdmen of Abram's cattle and the herdmen of Lot's cattle: and the Canaanite and the Perizzite dwelled then in the land.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Pressure on the land turns into open quarrel: “there was a strife between the herdmen of Abram’s cattle and the herdmen of Lot’s cattle.” The dispute begins among the servants, who would have competed for the best grazing and the first turn at the wells, each group eager to see its own master’s animals thrive. Quarrels over water and pasture recur throughout the patriarchal stories (21:25; 26:20–22). The masters are not yet said to be at odds, but quarrels among servants seldom stay below the surface for long, and the tension doubtless reflected attitudes higher up.

The narrator then adds a brief note: “the Canaanite and the Perizzite dwelled then in the land.” This explains why space was so tight. Abram and Lot were not alone on empty hills; the towns and fields already belonged to others, and the newcomers had to graze where they could. The Perizzites do not appear in the table of nations, and their name may describe people living in open, unwalled settlements, set beside the Canaanites of the fortified towns. Together they represent the settled population whose presence limited the newcomers.

The remark carries a second weight. The quarrel was taking place in full view of the people of the land. Abram had built altars and called on the LORD’s name among them; a family feud between the worshippers of the true God would undermine that witness. When believers fight among themselves before unbelieving neighbours, the name they profess is dishonoured (1 Corinthians 6:6–7). Jesus made love among his disciples the sign by which the world would recognise them (John 13:35). The presence of the Canaanite and the Perizzite made peace between Abram and Lot a matter of testimony as well as family harmony.

wordNotes.explanation: Riv denotes a quarrel or dispute, whether a heated argument or a formal complaint. In the prophets the word can describe the LORD’s case against his people, but here it refers to a quarrel settled directly between the parties, with no judge involved. The verb from the same root describes the herdmen of Gerar who “did strive” with Isaac’s servants over wells.

The Perizzites appear repeatedly among the peoples of Canaan, often paired with the Canaanites, yet they are absent from the genealogy of Canaan’s sons. Their name resembles perazi, “open country” or “unwalled village,” which suggests rural inhabitants rather than a distinct ethnic line, though certainty is not possible.

verses.bibleText: And Abram said unto Lot, Let there be no strife, I pray thee, between me and thee, and between my herdmen and thy herdmen; for we be brethren.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abram takes the initiative: “Let there be no strife, I pray thee, between me and thee, and between my herdmen and thy herdmen.” He addresses the conflict at its root, naming the two levels at which it existed. The quarrel among the servants is treated as the concern of the masters; Abram does not dismiss it as a matter for hired hands, nor wait for it to grow. The small courtesy “I pray thee” turns what could have been a command from the head of the clan into a request between equals.

The ground of his appeal is kinship: “for we be brethren.” Lot was Abram’s nephew, the son of his dead brother Haran (11:27–28), and Abram had in effect been a father to him. The Hebrew reads literally “men, brothers,” a phrase that stresses close kindred. Abram refuses to let property set relatives against each other. In a book full of brothers who deceive, hate, and even kill one another, from Cain and Abel to Joseph and his brothers, this appeal stands out. “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!” (Psalm 133:1).

The contrast with the previous chapter is striking. In Egypt Abram feared, schemed, and protected himself at Sarai’s expense. Here, fresh from the altar at Bethel, he acts as a peacemaker who is prepared to lose for the sake of harmony. He was the elder, the leader, and the one to whom the land had been promised, yet he claims none of those privileges. Worship had reordered his priorities.

Abram’s son Isaac would later show the same spirit, yielding disputed wells and digging new ones until he found room (26:22). Jesus pronounced peacemakers blessed and called them children of God (Matthew 5:9), and Paul urged believers, as far as lies in them, to live peaceably with all (Romans 12:18). Abram’s words show that peace is often purchased by the one with the stronger claim choosing not to press it.

wordNotes.explanation: Merivah is formed from the same root as riv in verse 7 and means contention or quarrelling. It later became the name of the place where Israel quarrelled with Moses and tested the LORD over water, “Meribah.” Here Abram uses it to name what he refuses to allow between himself and Lot.

wordNotes.term: אֲנָשִׁים אַחִים (ʾanashim ʾakhim) — we be brethren
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “men, brothers,” the phrase applies ʾakh in its broader sense of near kinsman, since Lot was Abram’s nephew. The word ʾakh covers full brothers, relatives, and fellow members of a people. Moses uses similar language when he tries to reconcile two quarrelling Hebrews.

verses.bibleText: Is not the whole land before thee? separate thyself, I pray thee, from me: if thou wilt take the left hand, then I will go to the right; or if thou depart to the right hand, then I will go to the left.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Is not the whole land before thee?” Abram’s proposal is simple and generous. Since the two households cannot remain together, they must part, and Lot may choose first. From the heights near Bethel the country spread out in every direction. If directions are reckoned facing east, as was common in the ancient Near East, “the left hand” was the north and “the right hand” the south. Whatever Lot selects, Abram will take the other.

The offer is remarkable because the land had been promised to Abram, not to Lot (12:7). By the custom of the time the elder would have chosen, and the junior would have accepted the remainder. Abram reverses the order. He risks, humanly speaking, the best of his inheritance, yet he does so without anxiety, because what God has promised cannot be lost by being yielded. A man secure in the promise does not need to grasp. Faith allowed Abram to let God, rather than his own shrewdness, determine what he would receive.

The word “separate” has a sober ring. The same verb describes the dividing of the nations after the flood (10:5, 32). Separation was the only way to preserve peace, and sometimes believers must part company so that strife does not continue (Acts 15:39). Yet it also meant that Lot would no longer live in the immediate company of the one through whom blessing flowed.

Some have suggested that Abram was careless with the promise in offering Lot any part of it. The narrative answers that objection, for the LORD speaks immediately afterward to renew and enlarge the promise (13:14–17). Abram’s self-giving points ahead to the mind of Christ, who did not regard his rights as something to cling to, but emptied himself and was afterward highly exalted (Philippians 2:5–9).

wordNotes.term: הִפָּרֶד נָא (hippared naʾ) — separate thyself, I pray thee
wordNotes.explanation: The reflexive stem of parad means to part company or be divided. It is used of the spreading of the nations and of the river parting into four heads. Proverbs uses it of the person who isolates himself in pursuit of his own desire. The particle naʾ softens the imperative into a courteous request.

verses.bibleText: And Lot lifted up his eyes, and beheld all the plain of Jordan, that it was well watered every where, before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, even as the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt, as thou comest unto Zoar.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Lot does not hesitate or defer to his uncle. “Lot lifted up his eyes, and beheld all the plain of Jordan, that it was well watered every where.” From the ridge near Bethel the eye could follow the descent toward the Jordan rift, the deepest valley on earth, where the river winds through a warm basin far below sea level. Springs and streams fed by the eastern highlands kept the lower valley green when the hill country waited on uncertain rain. To a herdsman who had just lived through a famine, abundant water was the decisive attraction.

The narrator interrupts the description with an ominous parenthesis: “before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah.” Readers already know what Lot did not. The lush plain he admires will become a place of fire and ruin (19:24–25). By setting the coming judgment in the middle of the description, the text warns that appearances can deceive and that the most attractive prospect may lie under the shadow of divine judgment.

Two comparisons follow. The plain was “even as the garden of the LORD,” that is, like Eden, watered by its river (2:10). It was also “like the land of Egypt,” fertile through the Nile, which Lot had recently seen. Both comparisons carry warning. Eden was the place where the first human pair saw what was desirable and took it (3:6), and the verb “beheld” here follows the same pattern of seeing that leads to taking. Egypt was the land where Abram had just compromised his integrity for safety and gain. Moses later reminded Israel that Canaan was unlike Egypt; it drank rain from heaven and depended on the LORD’s care (Deuteronomy 11:10–12). Lot preferred a land that seemed independent of such dependence.

The last phrase, “as thou comest unto Zoar,” marks the southern extent of the plain. Zoar, probably near the southeastern end of the Dead Sea, would later be the small town where Lot took refuge (19:20–23). The verse portrays a choice made by sight alone, without reference to God, to the moral character of the people, or to the counsel of the man through whom blessing came. The “lust of the eyes” (1 John 2:16) is not the only motive in Lot’s heart, but it governs the choice. Lot chose what looked like paradise; Abram, by faith, would look for a city whose builder and maker is God (Hebrews 11:10).

wordNotes.term: כִּכַּר הַיַּרְדֵּן (kikkar hayyarden) — the plain of Jordan
wordNotes.explanation: Kikkar means something round, such as a loaf or a disc-shaped talent of metal, and in geography an oval district. Applied to the Jordan, it describes the broad, rounded basin of the lower valley near the Dead Sea. It is used again for the area of the cities Lot settles among and the region the LORD overthrew.

wordNotes.term: כְּגַן־יְהוָה (kegan-YHWH) — as the garden of the LORD
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase refers to Eden, the garden planted by the LORD and watered by a river. Elsewhere Eden becomes the standard for fertility and for restored blessing. The comparison praises the plain’s richness while recalling the garden where desire first led to disobedience.

verses.bibleText: Then Lot chose him all the plain of Jordan; and Lot journeyed east: and they separated themselves the one from the other.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Then Lot chose him all the plain of Jordan.” The Hebrew says that Lot chose for himself, and the phrase captures the spirit of the decision. He takes the whole of the valley, not merely a share, and he does so without courtesy toward his elder, without consulting the LORD, and without concern for where his uncle would be left. Lot was not an idolater, and Scripture later calls him a righteous man (2 Peter 2:7). Yet in this hour his choice was guided by advantage. Lot’s decision fits his circumstances as a herdsman, which is why it was so easily made; that is often how the most consequential errors look at the time.

“And Lot journeyed east.” In Genesis eastward movement often signals distance from God’s presence. Adam and Eve were driven out to the east of Eden (3:24), Cain went east to Nod (4:16), and the builders of Babel journeyed from the east into Shinar (11:2). Lot’s move toward the sunrise takes him down from the hills where Abram worshipped and out toward the region of the cities.

“And they separated themselves the one from the other.” Literally, they parted, each man from his brother, the same word Abram had used for kinsmen in verse 8. The separation solved the immediate quarrel, but it removed Lot from the company and influence of the man through whom God had promised blessing. Choices made for comfort can reshape a whole family’s future. Lot’s descendants, the Moabites and Ammonites, would trace their origin to the aftermath of this move (19:36–38).

Moses would later choose differently, “esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt” (Hebrews 11:26). The contrast between Lot and Moses shows that every choice of residence and association is also a choice about what one values most.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb bakhar means to choose or select, often after examining options. The added lo, “for himself,” highlights self-interest; the KJV’s “chose him” preserves that idiom. The same verb appears when the sons of God took wives of all whom “they chose,” another instance where seeing leads to choosing.

Qedem means the front or the east, because the ancient observer oriented himself facing the sunrise. The preposition min often means “from,” but with directions it indicates the side or direction, here “eastward.” The same expression locates the garden and describes the movement toward Babel.

verses.bibleText: Abram dwelled in the land of Canaan, and Lot dwelled in the cities of the plain, and pitched his tent toward Sodom.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Verse 12 sets the two men side by side: “Abram dwelled in the land of Canaan, and Lot dwelled in the cities of the plain.” In Hebrew both names stand at the head of their clauses, inviting comparison. Abram remains within the land of promise, while Lot settles on its edge in the district of the cities. The verb “dwell,” which was twice negated in verse 6, can now be used of each man, but only because they live apart.

The final phrase is telling: Lot “pitched his tent toward Sodom.” He did not move into the city at once. He began as a herdsman camping near it, moving his tent by stages ever closer. Soon he is said to dwell in Sodom (14:12), and later he sits in its gate, the place of civic standing and business (19:1). The progression illustrates how compromise usually advances: first proximity, then residence, then involvement. The first Psalm traces a similar descent from walking, to standing, to sitting with the ungodly (Psalm 1:1).

Abram, by contrast, remains a tent-dweller for the rest of his life. Hebrews interprets this as a deliberate testimony of faith: he “sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country, dwelling in tabernacles,” because he looked for a lasting city built by God (Hebrews 11:9–10). Lot’s tent faced the city of men; Abram’s tent stood near the altar.

Scripture does not portray Lot as wholly lost. Peter says that righteous Lot was “vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked” and tormented in soul by what he saw and heard day after day (2 Peter 2:7–8). His conscience was not dead. Yet the choice to live near Sodom cost him his property, his influence, his wife, and the moral integrity of his family. Believers who settle near what grieves them may find that they can neither change it nor escape its influence unharmed.

wordNotes.term: וַיֶּאֱהַל עַד־סְדֹם (wayyeʾehal ʿad-Sedom) — and pitched his tent toward Sodom
wordNotes.explanation: The verb ʾahal is formed from ʾohel, “tent,” and means to pitch or move one’s tent; outside this chapter it appears only rarely. The preposition ʿad usually means “as far as” or “up to,” indicating that Lot’s camping range extended to the very edge of Sodom. Some render the clause as acquiring pasture up to the city. Either way, the phrase marks the boundary Lot was willing to approach.

verses.bibleText: But the men of Sodom were wicked and sinners before the LORD exceedingly.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Having placed Lot’s tent at the edge of Sodom, the narrator pauses to describe its people: “the men of Sodom were wicked and sinners before the LORD exceedingly.” The sentence is heavy with emphasis. They were evil, they were sinners, and their guilt was “exceedingly” great. This is the second ominous aside in the passage, matching the note about the coming destruction in verse 10. Together they frame Lot’s choice and show what he overlooked or chose to disregard.

The wickedness of Sodom was not a later development. It already existed when Lot drew near. Ezekiel lists the city’s sins as pride, fulness of bread, abundance of idleness, neglect of the poor and needy, and abominations (Ezekiel 16:49–50), and chapter 19 exposes its violence and sexual depravity. The very fertility that drew Lot had fed self-indulgence. Plenty that is received without gratitude easily becomes forgetfulness of God (Deuteronomy 8:12–14; Hosea 13:6).

The phrase “before the LORD” or “against the LORD” shows that the men of Sodom, though outside the covenant line and outside Canaan proper, were accountable to the God of Abram. His moral government reaches every nation. Their city would become, as Peter writes, an example to those who afterward live ungodly, reduced to ashes under judgment (2 Peter 2:6).

wordNotes.term: רָעִים וְחַטָּאִים לַיהוָה מְאֹד (raʿim wekhattaʾim laYHWH meʾod) — wicked and sinners before the LORD exceedingly
wordNotes.explanation: Raʿ is the broad word for what is evil or harmful, and khattaʾ describes one who misses the mark and offends, here plainly against God. The preposition le, “to” or “against the LORD,” makes God the offended party. Meʾod, “very,” intensifies the description, which anticipates the great outcry against Sodom in 18:20.

verses.bibleText: And the LORD said unto Abram, after that Lot was separated from him, Lift up now thine eyes, and look from the place where thou art northward, and southward, and eastward, and westward:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Now, for the first time in the chapter, the LORD speaks: “And the LORD said unto Abram, after that Lot was separated from him.” The time note is deliberate. Abram had heard no recorded word from God since he first arrived in the land (12:7), through the famine, the descent into Egypt, and the return. The divine voice comes only after the peacemaking and the parting. God now addresses the man who has just given up the first choice, and he speaks to assure him that nothing has been lost.

“Lift up now thine eyes, and look.” The language echoes verse 10 exactly. Lot lifted up his eyes on his own initiative and saw a valley he could take for himself. Abram lifts up his eyes at the LORD’s command and sees a land he will receive as a gift. The posture is the same; the difference lies in who directs the looking. Lot saw by appetite, Abram by promise. The small Hebrew word rendered “now” carries the sense of a gracious request, and it is rare for God to address a person this way. He uses it when he asks for faith in something beyond human reckoning, as when he tells Abram to count the stars (15:5) and to take his son to Moriah (22:2).

“From the place where thou art” means from the heights near Bethel, beside the altar. From there Abram is told to look northward, southward, eastward, and westward. The view includes the very valley Lot had chosen, for Lot’s portion, too, lies within what God is giving. In the ancient world a property could be conveyed by showing it to the new owner, and the LORD later gave Moses a similar view of the whole land from Mount Nebo (Deuteronomy 34:1–4). Jacob, at this same Bethel, would hear the promise that his seed would spread to the west, east, north, and south (28:14).

The scene shows God’s timing and kindness. The one who yields is not left poorer. Jesus promised that those who give up houses or lands for his sake will receive far more (Mark 10:29–30). Abram had let Lot choose; God now chooses for Abram, and his choice is everything.

wordNotes.term: שָׂא־נָא עֵינֶיךָ (sa-naʾ ʿeneykha) — lift up now thine eyes
wordNotes.explanation: The idiom “lift up the eyes” means to look attentively into the distance. It deliberately repeats the wording of Lot’s look in verse 10. The particle naʾ adds courtesy or entreaty and is seldom used by God when speaking to a human being; its presence here marks an invitation to trust rather than a bare order.

Maqom is the ordinary word for place or site, but in the Abram narratives it repeatedly marks locations of worship and encounter with God, such as Shechem, Bethel, and Moriah. Its recurrence in verses 3, 4, and 14 ties the promise to the altar where Abram had renewed his worship.

verses.bibleText: For all the land which thou seest, to thee will I give it, and to thy seed for ever.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“For all the land which thou seest, to thee will I give it, and to thy seed for ever.” The promise of 12:7 is renewed and enlarged. Previously God had said, “Unto thy seed will I give this land.” Now Abram himself is included: “to thee … and to thy seed.” The scope is “all the land” within sight in every direction, and the duration is “for ever.” Lot had chosen one valley; God gives Abram the whole.

The inclusion of Abram personally raises a question that Scripture itself answers. Abraham never owned more of Canaan than a burial cave, which he had to purchase (23:16–20). Stephen says God “gave him none inheritance in it, no, not so much as to set his foot on,” and yet promised to give it to him (Acts 7:5). Hebrews explains that the patriarchs “died in faith, not having received the promises,” confessing that they were strangers and pilgrims, because they desired “a better country, that is, an heavenly” (Hebrews 11:13–16). A promise made to a man who died without receiving it can be fulfilled only by God raising him from the dead and bringing him into the inheritance. Abraham’s hope looked beyond his own lifetime to the resurrection and the restored earth.

Paul draws out the meaning of “thy seed.” He observes that the promise speaks of seed in the singular and identifies that Seed as Christ (Galatians 3:16). Those who belong to Christ are therefore “Abraham’s seed, and heirs according to the promise” (Galatians 3:29). Paul can even describe the promise as making Abraham “the heir of the world” (Romans 4:13), in harmony with Jesus’ word that the meek shall inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5). The land promise widens into the hope of the new earth in which righteousness dwells (2 Peter 3:13).

“For ever” expresses the permanence of God’s commitment, yet within the covenant the enjoyment of the land by Abraham’s physical descendants was bound up with faithfulness. Moses warned that Israel would be removed from the land if it turned to idols (Deuteronomy 4:25–27), and that happened in the exile. The unconditional certainty lies in God’s purpose to give the inheritance to Abraham’s true seed. That purpose stands, and it is fulfilled in Christ and in all who share Abraham’s faith, whether born of his line or grafted in through the gospel.

wordNotes.explanation: Zeraʿ means seed sown in the ground and, by extension, offspring. It is a collective singular that can refer to many descendants or to one individual, as in the promise of the woman’s seed. Paul builds on this flexibility when he identifies the promised seed with Christ, while also including all who are Christ’s.

ʿOlam denotes a long or unbounded duration whose limits lie beyond view; its extent is governed by the subject it describes. It can mean lifelong service, the perpetual duration of an ordinance, or the everlasting nature of God. Applied to the land, it stresses the enduring certainty of God’s gift, which reaches its fullness in the eternal inheritance of the saints.

verses.bibleText: And I will make thy seed as the dust of the earth: so that if a man can number the dust of the earth, then shall thy seed also be numbered.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And I will make thy seed as the dust of the earth.” Promise of offspring follows promise of land, because a vast territory requires a vast people. The words are bold, since Abram was childless and Sarai barren (11:30). God had already said he would make of Abram a great nation (12:2); now he says the nation will be beyond counting. The comparison to dust is followed by a gentle challenge: if anyone could number the dust of the earth, then Abram’s seed could be numbered too.

The imagery will vary as the promise is repeated: stars of heaven (15:5), sand on the seashore (22:17). Each pictures a multitude that only God can count. There may also be a wordplay. The “earth” (ʾerets) whose dust measures Abram’s descendants is the same word as the “land” promised to them in verses 15 and 17. Balaam later marvelled, “Who can count the dust of Jacob?” (Numbers 23:10). The final fulfilment is the redeemed company that John saw, “a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations” (Revelation 7:9).

wordNotes.term: כַּעֲפַר הָאָרֶץ (kaʿafar haʾarets) — as the dust of the earth
wordNotes.explanation: ʿAfar is fine dry soil or dust, the material from which the man was formed. Here it serves as a picture of countless quantity. The same promise is repeated to Jacob, and Solomon later describes Israel as a people “like the dust of the earth in multitude.”

verses.bibleText: Arise, walk through the land in the length of it and in the breadth of it; for I will give it unto thee.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Arise, walk through the land in the length of it and in the breadth of it.” God invites Abram to move from looking to walking. Having seen the land from Bethel, he is to travel through it in every direction, the way an owner inspects his estate. The command implies possession: no one surveys property as his own unless he believes it is his. Ancient rulers sometimes marked their claim to a territory by passing through it or around its borders, and the LORD would later tell Joshua that every place where Israel’s feet trod had been given to them (Joshua 1:3).

The reason is repeated: “for I will give it unto thee.” Nothing in Abram’s walking earned the land; the walk was a response of faith to a gift already pledged. Abram did not conquer anything or displace anyone. He moved through the country as a guest of its present inhabitants, carrying the word of God as his only title deed. That is how faith lives: it acts on what God has said before the fulfilment is visible.

The verb “walk” in this form means to walk about or go to and fro, and it is the same form used for Enoch and Noah, who “walked with God” (5:24; 6:9). The LORD would soon call Abram to “walk before me, and be thou perfect” (17:1). Walking through the land and walking before God belong together. Believers today also walk in the promises, living now as heirs of what they have not yet seen (2 Corinthians 5:7).

wordNotes.explanation: Qum, “arise,” often introduces decisive action. Hithallekh is the reflexive-iterative form of halakh, “to go,” meaning to walk about, move back and forth, or conduct one’s life. It describes Enoch and Noah walking with God and the patrol of the land by Joshua’s surveyors. Here it calls Abram to traverse the country as one who owns it by promise.

verses.bibleText: Then Abram removed his tent, and came and dwelt in the plain of Mamre, which is in Hebron, and built there an altar unto the LORD.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abram obeys. “Then Abram removed his tent, and came and dwelt in the plain of Mamre, which is in Hebron.” The verb for moving his tent is the same unusual word used of Lot’s camping toward Sodom in verse 12. The two men both pitch their tents, but in opposite directions and with opposite results. Lot moves toward a city whose people are exceedingly wicked; Abram moves south through the land God has given him and settles in the high hill country.

The word the KJV renders “plain” refers to large trees, the oaks or terebinths of Mamre. The grove took its name from Mamre the Amorite, who with his brothers Eshcol and Aner became Abram’s ally (14:13, 24). The friendship of these neighbours may reflect the character of Abram’s life among them. Hebron lay on the ridge route about twenty miles south of the later site of Jerusalem, one of the highest towns in the land. In Abram’s day it was known as Kirjath-arba (23:2), and Moses uses the later name his readers would recognise. It was an ancient city, built seven years before Zoan in Egypt (Numbers 13:22).

Hebron becomes the centre of the patriarchal story. From Mamre Abraham will receive the heavenly visitors and plead for Sodom (18:1, 22–33). Nearby he will buy the cave of Machpelah, where he, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob, and Leah are buried to await the fulfilment of the promise (23:17–20; 49:29–31). Centuries later Caleb would claim Hebron by faith (Joshua 14:13–14), and David would first reign there as king (2 Samuel 2:1–4).

The chapter ends where it began, at an altar: Abram “built there an altar unto the LORD.” The first altar in the chapter marked his return; this one marks his response to the renewed promise. Each altar declared his loyalty to the LORD amid neighbours who served other gods, and it made his camp a place of worship. Lot’s life gathered around a city; Abram’s gathered around the altar. That difference, more than any division of pasture, determined the outcome of the two men’s choices.

wordNotes.term: בְּאֵלֹנֵי מַמְרֵא (beʾelone mamreʾ) — in the plain of Mamre
wordNotes.explanation: ʾElon denotes a large tree, probably an oak or terebinth, prized for shade and often associated with sacred sites. The KJV’s “plain” follows an older rendering. The plural points to a grove. Such trees served as landmarks for meeting and worship, as at the oak of Moreh near Shechem.

Mizbeakh comes from the verb zavakh, “to slaughter for sacrifice,” and denotes the place of sacrificial worship. Abram’s altars at Shechem, Bethel, and Hebron mark the stages of his life in the land and testify publicly to the LORD who had appeared to him. They anticipate the sacrificial system and, beyond it, the one offering of Christ.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: When two good things compete for the same space, what decides who gets the better share?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: Abram, restored to worship, can yield his rights because God’s promise secures his future, while Lot’s choice by appearance leads him toward Sodom.
importantTerms: called on the name of the LORD
discussionQuestions: What does Abram’s return to the altar at Bethel suggest about recovery after failure?
Why did increasing wealth create conflict between Abram and Lot?
What gave Abram the freedom to let Lot choose first?
How do the narrator’s notes in verses 10 and 13 shape our view of Lot’s choice?
How does Hebrews 11 interpret Abram’s life in tents within the promised land?
commonMisunderstandings: Abram’s generosity did not earn the promise; God had already given it in 12:7 and simply renewed it.
Lot is not presented as an unbeliever; the New Testament calls him righteous, yet his choice exposed him and his family to grave harm.
The promise of the land “for ever” does not set aside the conditions of covenant faithfulness; its final fulfilment belongs to Abraham’s seed in Christ.
Walking through the land was not a magical claim but an act of faith in what God had spoken.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep the altars at the beginning and end in view: worship restores Abram’s perspective, and that perspective frees him to make peace and to trust God for his inheritance.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Return to the place where you first met God, refuse to fight for what he has already promised, and let his word rather than appearances guide your choices.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: God’s promise of an inheritance is received by faith, frees believers from grasping, and reaches its fulfilment in Christ and the restored earth.
flow: Abram failed in Egypt, yet God brought him back to the altar and he called on the LORD again.
Secure in God’s promise, Abram yielded his rights to keep peace with Lot.
Lot chose by what looked best and moved toward a city ripe for judgment.
God renewed the promise of land and offspring to Abram and his seed, whom Paul identifies with Christ.
All who belong to Christ share Abraham’s hope of an inheritance in the earth made new.
simpleIllustrations: A traveller who knows a house is waiting at the journey’s end does not quarrel over a seat in the waiting room.
A shopfront can be lit brilliantly while the business behind it is collapsing; Lot judged the plain by its frontage.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you trust God’s promise enough to let go of what you are grasping and choose the path that keeps you near him?
cautions: Do not turn Abram into a model of flawless faith; the chapter follows directly on his failure in Egypt.
Do not use the land promise to support political claims; keep the focus on God’s faithfulness and the inheritance in Christ.
Do not present wealth itself as sinful; the danger lies in letting it decide where and with whom we live.

reflectionQuestions: Where do I need to return, as Abram returned to Bethel, to the place where I first called on God?
What right am I holding so tightly that it keeps me in strife with someone close to me?
When I last made a major decision, did I weigh what it would do to my walk with God and my family?
Am I pitching my tent toward a place whose values I know are opposed to God?
How does God’s promise of a final inheritance change the way I handle what I own now?
